front: The lawsuit defense of {{c1::governmental immunity::defense}} generally applies only to EMS systems operated by {{c1::municipalities or other governmental entities::operator type}}.
back_extra:
Meaning: if covered, the service sometimes cannot be sued at all (particularly when an emergency exists), or the plaintiff's monetary judgment may be capped.

Pitfall: state laws vary significantly on immunity, so learn the law where you work.

front: A patient tells you her religious convictions strongly oppose {{c1::medications, blood, and blood products::3 items}}. Beyond respecting her wishes, you must {{c2::report the objection to the next level of care::action}}.
back_extra:
Why: the objection can only be honored after handoff if the information travels with the patient — respecting it yourself is not enough.

Ex: other religious needs to respect in the field: patients may cling to medals or charms (especially if you attempt to remove them), and may ask for religious counsel, baptism, or last rites when death is imminent — try to accommodate these requests.

front:
Medical errors are examined as coming from three possible sources (alone or combined):
{{c1::rules-based failure::r}}
{{c1::knowledge-based failure::k}}
{{c1::skills-based failure::s}}
back_extra:
Cue: the three map to authority (rules), information (knowledge), and hands-on execution (skills).

Distinguish: giving a drug without the legal right or the medical director's permission is a rules-based failure - even if the drug was correct - not a knowledge-based one.
